title: First assessment of the genetic structure of deepwater blackmouth catshark (Galeus melastomus Rafinesque, 1810) in Atlantic and Mediterranean populations
abstract_text: The worldwide abundance of Galeus melastomus in the biological composition of fishery bycatch led to consider this species as a key-taxon for understanding the mysterious biology and ecology of sharks living in deep ecosystems. With the present work, we aim to unravel the population structure of the blackmouth catshark in the Mediterranean Sea and adjacent North-Eastern Atlantic with the use of nuclear molecular markers (simple sequence repeats, SSRs) and compare our results with recent findings based on mitochondrial DNA supporting total panmixia in the species. Given the absence of species-specific microsatellite markers we attempted the cross-amplification of a panel of 129 SSRs developed for Centroselachus crepidater, Galeorhinus galeus, Hexanchus griseus, Mustelus antarcticus, M. canis, M. henlei, M. mustelus, Negaprion brevirostris, Scyliorhinus canicula, Squalus acanthias and S. mitsukurii on blackmouth catsharks collected during scientific surveys undertaken in different years. The rationale of the chosen methodology was based on the calculation of genetic distances between NADH2 sequences (1044bp long) derived from 595 species of elasmobranchs. Our strategy focused on testing first SSRs markers developed on closely-related species. Then, we assessed highly polymorphic markers developed on non-closely-related species. After a pilot gradient amplification on few individuals from three different geographic macro-areas, we screened a total of 24 samples at the established conditions. To date, 16 microsatellite loci have been classified as potential candidates for the successful cross-amplification on Atlantic and Mediterranean samples of G. melastomus. These candidate loci will be applied in the population genetic analysis delineated in the Atlantic Ocean (two sites) and in the Mediterranean Sea (five sites). Hopefully, the higher resolution power of the markers chosen for this study will be able to disclose any signal of genetic structure of the blackmouth catsharks and will contribute to improve the knowledge on deep-sharks.

title: Recent attacks by White Shark in the Strait of Messina
abstract_text: According to Boldrocchi et alii (2017) the information on the diet of white sharks in the Mediterranean inferred from stomach content analyses of 103 stomachs revealed among other prey items 45 bony fish and 5 cartilaginous fish. The most common teleost prey groups were tuna (Thunnus spp.) and swordfish (Xiphias gladius). In the Strait of Messina motorboats known as "feluche" or are used to catch the swordfish. These have a 20-25 m high mast, on the top of which sighters and helmsmen are placed: on the front there is a walkway up to 45 m long, at the end of which the harpooner is standing. In this sector of the sea, the press often reports the presence of large sharks. In the present note we report three shark attacks (documented by photographs) on Red Tuna and Swordfish in the Strait. On April 5, 2017, during the ascent of a 70 kg line-caught red tuna, a white shark launched an attack that documented a bite that removed about 30 kg of flesh from the ventral region. The second attack took place on August 1, 2019 in the water in front of S. Agata of Messina on a swordfish hooked by a feluca, "Felicia II"; the swordfish after being harpooned fell to the sea bottom at a depth 80 metres, where it remained for about 20 minutes. Subsequently the fish it was set on board allowing to record a bite that ha detached about 20 kg of flesh, the entire weight of the fish was estimated at around 107 kg. The third attack was observed by the same fishermen on August 5, 2019. A swordfish swimming below the surface was successfully attacked by a white shark which cut off its tail. The same swordfish was subsequently harpooned and hoisted on board on the feluca.

title: An updated check-list of elasmobranchs of Calabria
abstract_text: Despite Calabria represents an interesting study area due to its geographic position, nothing is known of the presence of sharks and rays in this region. Data presented in this work come from nineteen years of opportunistic fishing surveys (from 2000 to 2019). Our data shows that 53 species of elasmobranchs are present in Calabrian seas: 30 of these are sharks, 22 are rays. To these, 1 species of Chimaeras must be added. All they represent about the 50% of species reported for the Mediterranean. The more widespread encountered species were Hexanchus griseus, Scyliorhinus canicula, Prionace glauca, Raja asterias and Raja clavata. Very interesting is also the presence and distribution in the study area of species such as Cetorhinus maximus, Carcharodon carcharias, Isurus oxyrhincus, Sphyrna zygaena and Mobula mobular. Also, information on localities and specimens has been presented. We report also new records of Alopias superciliosus, Carcharhinus obscurus and Sphyrna mokarran.

title: The diet of deep-sea sharks
abstract_text: The deep-sea can be defined as the part of the oceans below 200 meters. The organisms living there can be qualified as deep-sea organisms. However, a lot of these organisms display vertical movements bringing them above 200 meters, making it difficult to classify them. Deep-sea organisms are thus considered here to be organisms spending most of their life cycle below 200 meters. Due to the technical difficulties linked to deep-sea study, a lot remains to be discovered about the organisms living in the depths of the oceans. The trophic structure and interactions inside the deep-sea food-webs remain poorly known for a lot of taxa, including deep-sea sharks. Here, we first try to separate the known shark species between deep-sea and surface species. We then try to review the available knowledges on deep-sea sharks' diet. Most of the information come from stomach contents but the use of more recent techniques is increasing in order to assess deep-sea sharks' trophic ecology. Stable isotope analyzes and fatty acid profiles have proved to provide useful information in this regard and have been included in our review.

title: Effect of environmental and temporal variables on the relative abundance of Carcharhinus falciformis and Sphyrna zygaena in Cabo San Lucas, Mexico
abstract_text: Environmental factors have an important effect on sharks. It has been observed that the horizontal and vertical movements of these animals, as well as their distribution, abundance, and use of habitat, can be influenced by biotic and abiotic factors. Due to the fact that pelagic sharks possess specific environmental preferences, and the area of Cabo San Lucas is characterized by drastic oceanographic variability between the warm and temperate seasons, we expect the relative abundance of these organisms to be influenced by environmental factors, especially temperature and chlorophyll concentration. The main goal of this study was to determine which environmental and temporal variables (month and hour) have significant influence over the relative abundance of Carcharhinus falciformis and Sphyrna zygaena in Cabo San Lucas. To do this, submarine censuses were completed, where we registered the relative abundance of these species, as well as environmental factors such as sea surface temperature, wind speed, and water color. Also, satellite data regarding chlorophyll a concentration was downloaded. These variables were incorporated into generalized linear models (GLM), where the relative abundance was the response factor. For C. falciformis, we found significant differences for temperature, chlorophyll concentration, month of the year, and hour (GLM, p<0.001). Its relative abundance was greater with warm waters (29.7±0.3ºC), whereas it was lower with high concentrations of chlorophyll (0.15±0.002 mg/m3). Also, they were more abundant during Autumn and between 5 and 6 pm. In contrast, water color was the only variable that showed significant differences for S. zygaena (GLM, p<0.01), with green water resulting in greater relative abundance. This is the first study to characterize the abundance and temporality of two highly exploited shark species in the region, and we found differences amongst them. Our results give valuable information in terms of management and conservation efforts in the area.

title: Preliminary data on population trends of Great White Shark, Carcharodon carcharias (Linnaeus, 1758), in Gansbaai (Southafrica) between 2009 and 2019
abstract_text: Since 2000, the CSS team (Sharks Studies Center), as part of the project: "Ecology and Ethology of the Great White Shark", has been collecting ethological data during Scientific Expeditions organized in South Africa in Gansbaai, 200 km east of Cape Town. In Gansbaai Bay and around Dyer Island and Geyser rock, there is a large population of White Sharks that can be observed thanks to the support of local ecotourism operators authorized to reach the best field observation sites. Research activities about ethological and ecotoxicological analyses, covered between 2003 and 2019, were developed in collaboration with: University of Calabria and Siena in Italy and Stellenbosch University in South Africa. In order to enable proper data collection, it was necessary to develop techniques to identify white sharks that consist mainly of the collection of various biometric and environmental data in special sheets, as well as photographs of animals with special attention to the dorsal fins. After the first years of optimization of the techniques and of staff involved, it was necessary to identify the individual specimens and, between 2009 and 2019, it was possible to create a db. Since 2009 to 2019, between march and may, 423 different white sharks were catalogued for a total of 440 hours of field observations from the boat and 220 hours of observations from the cage, including 99 photographs of unique dorsal fins. In this work the preliminary results, related to the trends of the population present in Gansbaai Bay are presented and discussed.

title: Sharks in hot waters: effects of a simulated marine heatwave over the foraging behaviour of a temperate catshark
abstract_text: Marine heatwaves (MHWs) are known to have large-scale implications over entire ecosystems, however, their effects over key predators, such as elasmobranchs, are still poorly understood. Although multiples studies have revealed several developmental, physiological, and behavioural implications of temperature increase in this group, this has yet to be addressed in an MHW context. In the present study, we investigated the effects of a simulated MHW over the foraging behaviour of juvenile temperate sharks (Scyliorhinus canicula). Treatment conditions were chosen to reflect a realist MHW scenario based on previous events detected in the wild (15 days, Δ 3 °C above climatological normal; category II). Following exposure, the animal food intake, foraging motivation and response to both olfactory and electrical cues were assessed. While no changes were observed in food intake, cue response, and foraging time, there was an increase in the number of turns and biting events. These behavioural changes may indicate changes in foraging efficiency, which not only have the potential to undermine the coping capacity of shark juveniles but also to induce changes in the predation dynamics. As anthropogenic climate change continues unabated, MHWs are expected to increase in frequency, duration and intensity, which may further challenge the foraging efficiency of these key predators, with potential cascading consequences in ecosystems already subjected increasing pressure.

title: Behavioural complexity in white sharks: influence of age, sex and environment
abstract_text: From 2005 to 2018 the individual surface behaviour of bait-attracted white sharks during ecotourism activites has been studied off Dyer Island Nature Reserve (South Africa). Observations were made from a commercial cage-diving boat both by observers and by a drone. A total of 235 white sharks has been identified. The individual behavioural units observed were: parading, bait following, visual inspection, breach, tail slap, tail stand, spy hop, repetitive aerial gaping, and head-up vertical emerging. We compared the exhibition of these behaviors and the complexity of the ethograms to both biological (sex, age) and environmental (tides, cloud cover, underwater visibility, sea surface conditions, temperature, time of the day) factors. We observed no correlation between behavior and sex of the white sharks, while a significant correlation was observed comparing ethograms of mature and immature white sharks: young sharks performed more complex ethograms with a higher number of behavioural units than adult ones. Regarding the effects of environmental conditions, the sequence and structure of individual behaviors were affected in particular by cloud cover and tides.

title: Occurrence of the basking shark (Cetorhinus maximus) in French waters. 20 years of data from a public sightings recording scheme
abstract_text: Since 1998, a public basking shark sightings recording scheme is established in French waters. The aim is to gather simple data on occurrences to locate any sightings hotspots and, in the long term, to detect possible variations in spatial and seasonal distribution of the sightings. Highlighting such areas could help to minimize conflict between this species of conservation concern and human activities. This type of projects involving members of the public are recognised for contributing also in terms of public awareness. This is something important to make possible the implementation of new measures to better protect basking sharks. We analysed data collected between 1998 and 2017 (20 years). 1857 sightings representing 2409 sharks were recorded. Data were analysed in term of spatial, inter-annual and seasonal distribution. Inter-annual and seasonal distribution were investigated globally and for several geographical areas (Mediterranean Sea, Bay of Biscay, Celtic Sea, Channel and south North Sea).

title: First insights into the trophic ecology of young White Sharks (Carcharodon carcharias) in Baja California waters, Mexico
abstract_text: White sharks are usually defined as generalist predators, with a well described ontogenetic dietary shift that occurs between the subadult and adult stages. Yet the majority of published studies have focused on large and mature individuals, so the information about feeding habits is still lacking for young white sharks. It is imperative to improve information about the trophic ecology of white sharks across life-stages to better understand habitat shifts and their early life movements inside nursery areas, which are determined by resources availability. This study provides the first insight into the trophic ecology of young white sharks using stable isotopes analysis (SIA) in muscle tissues to characterize prey contributions and ontogenetic changes in habitat use. We collected muscle of 21 white sharks from Sebastian Vizcaino Bay (SVB) during the period 2015-2018, including five newborns, three YOY and three juveniles. White shark isotopic values did not vary by sex (δ15N values: W = 52, p = 0.8 and δ13C values: t = 0.25, p = 0.8) as well as age classes (δ15N values: W =54, p = 0.4 and δ13C values: t = -0.9, p = 0.4) and we did not find variation based on size classes for δ13C and δ15N. However, we found changes in prey composition across white shark life stages, with significant changes throughout ontogeny. Mixing model indicate a high use of coastal areas for foraging, which likely represents the shift from the embryo's typical maternally-derived isotopic signature incorporated in offshore foraging regions to the postpartum isotopic composition, incorporated by neonates from inshore nursery habitats, including SVB. This study reinforces the assertion that coastal areas, like SVB and the prey preferences that take place in this area (from previous research) are critical for the development and to the successful foraging of young white sharks, providing relevant knowledge regarding this species.

title: Composition of the diet of three Etmopterus species off Angola
abstract_text: Three species of lantern sharks occur in Angolan waters: Etmopterus polli, E. pusillus, and E. spinax, along the continental slope at depths down to 1000 m. As part of the regional cooperation between Norway and Angola annual surveys were carried out on board the R/V Dr Fridtjof Nansen. During these surveys, 4162 individuals were collected, Total length (TL), sex, maturity and stomach content were recorded. The specimen's length range was: 10 to 27 cm TL for E. polli, 10 to 55 cm TL for E. pusillus and 10 to 35 cm TL for E. spinax. Food items were identified to the lowest possibly taxon, weighed, measured and grouped into three taxonomic groups: teleosts, cephalopods, crustaceans and remains (e.g. squid beaks, scales and otoliths). Prey importance was evaluated by using the index of relative importance (IRI), expressed as percentage (%IRI). To determine if there were significant differences in stomach contents between sexes and maturity stages, multivariate analysis of variance (MANOVA) were done. The dependent variable used was the Index of Relative Fullness (IRF). Preliminary results show that these species consumed a relatively wide range of prey items belonging to three major groups: teleosts (10 families), crustaceans (7 families), and cephalopods (4 families). For all three Etmopterus species, cephalopods were the most frequent prey. The other categories varied in importance in the diet by species and life history stage. There were no significant differences in the diet of males and females, but we found an ontogenetic dietary shift, reflected in the importance of teleosts between immature and mature specimens. E. polli had the highest dietary diversity and seem to feed mainly on fast moving prey. This study provides the first quantitative investigation of the diets of three species of sharks belonging to the Etmopteridae family off Angola.

title: Organochlorine compounds in several species of shark sampled in three different world areas
abstract_text: Persistent organic pollutants (POPs) such as organochlorine compounds (OCs) are still exploited in some countries both for special permit and for the non-regulation of these products. Marine apex predators like sharks have the potential to accumulate and biomagnify OCs due to their position in the trophic food web. In this study we analyzed hexachlorobenzene (HCB), dichlorodiphenyltrichloroethane and its metabolites (DDTs) and polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs) in 59 muscle samples from by-caught and free ranging sharks of 6 different species collected in 3 different areas: Mediterranean Sea, northern New South Wales (Australia) and Dyer Island (South Africa). Overall, South African specimens were the most impacted by PCBs and Mediterranean species by DDTs. Nevertheless, ratio between pp'DDE/pp'DDT in South African sharks suggested a recent use of this xenobiotic along with DDT fingerprint in Australian specimens, while unusually high values of op' DDT isomers are probably linked to the use of an industrial (non-insecticidal) DDT.

title: From purse seine bycatch data to population trends: deriving an abundance index for the silky shark based on its associative behaviour with floating objects in the Indian Ocean
abstract_text: Classified as vulnerable to near-threatened on the IUCN red list, the silky shark, Carcharhinus falciformis is a pelagic species. The species is vulnerable to overfishing due to its spatial distribution and biological characteristic. Using data from French and Spanish tropical tuna purse seine fishery, this study proposes a new method to derive an abundance index for silky shark's populations in two areas of the Indian Ocean. Two models were used: the first one describes the dynamics of sharks associated to floating objects (FOBs) used by tuna purse seiners in a social and in a non-social case. The second one illustrates the exchanges of individuals between the FOB-associated population and an external pool of sharks. The parameters estimated of the first model were obtained with fitting analysis. They were then integrated to the second model, allowing to derive an abundance index for the silky shark in statistical units of space and time and therefore the construction of temporal series of the population trend. This methodology has the potential to be applied to many other species associating with FOBs and serve as a tool for fisheries management.

title: Challenging the data and status quo: the case of deepwater species in the high north – do we need dedicated elasmobranch surveys?
abstract_text: Deepwater species are in general more difficult to study compared to species in shallower waters due to the difficulty of access. This is limiting many studies to determining the presence and population composition at a very specific timepoint only, that is, the timepoint of catch, usually via a trawl. The power of such data therefore lies in the establishment of time series with many repeated measurements over a long time span, ideally also covering a large enough spatial area to capture the entire population range. We analysed >30 years of survey data from the Institute of Marine Research in Norway spanning minaly the North Sea and the Norwegian Sea focussing on deepsea sharks, skates and chimaera. We focussed on annual or bi-annual survey series that have been ongoing for at least 25 years. All survey series are designed to monitor the population status of commercial species like redfish, greenland halibut and shrimps and are based on trawl catches. Species-specific distributions, and changes over time, can be detected, as well as developments of population composition (e.g. size and gender) by such time series. However, critical information like presence/absence and continuous distribution along different habitat types are typically not possible to assess, and neither are "realistic" number for species not typically caught in trawls. We would like to present a few discussion points about the pro's and con's for dedicated chondrichthyan surveys and possible methodological additions to existing surveys, including the critical question about cost/benefit for e.g. rare, threatened or indicator species.

title: Using a coastal shark species as sentinel in marine pollution biomonitoring surveys
abstract_text: Marine contamination is worse than ever. To have an indication of stress or susceptibility, understanding how contamination correlates with key biological endpoints is essential. Sharks tend to accumulate high amounts of contaminants throughout their lives, bioaccumulating pollutants present in the water and biomagnifying the pollutants from their prey. Many shark species are caught and consumed all over the world, making them relevant for economical and public health reasons. To understand possible consequences of contamination, the present work aimed to quantify the levels of some metals in Scyliorhinus canicula and also measure biochemical biomarkers related with oxidative stress and energy metabolism. Moreover, efforts were made towards understating how the contamination-response patterns varied between lethal and less-invasive/non-lethal sampling. Sharks caught off the coast of Portugal by a commercial trawling boat were sampled. For each individual, levels of 13 metals were measured in both skin and muscle, while biochemical parameters were measured in several tissues including muscle, liver, blood and skin. Arsenic (As), iron (Fe), and zinc (Zn) had the higher mean values of all measured metals. There was a tendency for higher metal accumulation in skin, with differences being found between life-stages and genders. Furthermore, some analysed sharks surpassed stipulated guideline limits for human consumption of mercury (Hg) and As. Regarding the biochemical responses, suitable biomarker candidates could be identified as several significant correlations were observed between the physiological parameters and contaminant accumulation levels. When comparing lethal and non-lethal sampling some promising similarities were observed, especially when using skin biopsies, indicating good potential for being used as proxy for deeper tissues in future biomonitoring efforts. This study further highlights the effectiveness of combining biochemical parameters and pollutant body burden determinations to assess effects of contamination and demonstrates the great potential of sharks to be used in biomonitoring studies of the marine environment.

title: Half a century of global decline in oceanic sharks and rays
abstract_text: Overexploitation is the primary cause of fish extinction risk, yet individual species declines are difficult to track, particularly in the high seas. This knowledge gap impedes progress towards Aichi Biodiversity Targets and Sustainable Development Goals. We take advantage of newly available timeseries for 53 timeseries of 18 species of oceanic sharks and rays to measure changes in abundance by calculating the Living Planet Index. Worldwide, the abundance of oceanic sharks and rays has declined by 71% since 1970, with the steepest ongoing decline occurring in the Indian Ocean. Recent catch quotas, prohibitions, and international trade regulations provide some hope, yet without a drastic improvement in implementation of management there is a real risk of worldwide collapse of these populations and a disruption of their ecological function.

title: Bioaccumulation and trophic transfer of Cadmium in Brown smooth-hound Mustelus henlei in Las Barrancas, Baja California Sur, Mexico
abstract_text: We analyzed the concentration of cadmium in the mesopredator Mustelus henlei in an area influenced by a natural deposit of phosphorite and by coastal upwellings. Both processes provide Cd in a natural way. In the Las Barrancas, Mexico, M. henlei is one of the most important coastal sharks in the artisanal fishery of the region, representing an important source for human consumption. Due to the risk that it may constitute for human health, it is necessary to know the concentrations of Cd in muscle and liver, the risk to consumers and evaluate the biomagnification of this element in the trophic chain. The concentrations of Cd in the muscle of M. henlei were lower than the limits of detection, then the meat of this species does not constitute a risk to human health. However, the liver hade average concentrations of 0.96 µg g-1 (0-6.07, min-max), these values are above what is established by the official Mexican Norm, probably due to the high influence of the phosphorite deposits present, and to the upwelling events in the study area. The Mann-Whitney U test showed that had statistically significant differences in Cd between females 0.65 µg g-1 (0.26-4.85, min-max) and males 1.21 µg g-1 (0.43-6.07, min-max): this is probably ta consequence of the metabolic characteristics of each sex. The linear regression showed that there was no relationship between the length of M. henlei and the Cd concentration: this let speculate that probably there is no bioaccumulation of the Cd in the liver as the organisms increase in size. The analysis of Cd in the main prey of M. henlei using the factor of biomagnification (FBM) indicated that red crab (P. planipes) with respect to M. henlei was: FBM= 1.08; whereas the chub mackerel (S. japonicus) was 4.57, which indicates a higher biomagnification of this element in chub mackerel.

title: First determination of organochlorine pollutants (OCs) in oceanic manta rays, Mobula birostris
abstract_text: Oceanic manta rays Mobula birostris, are broadly distributed in tropical and temperate waters and their populations are in decline worldwide. In the Mexican Pacific Ocean, they are protected from fishing activity, with a permanent ban for their capture, possession and commerce in the whole country. For this reason, data on their ecology and toxicology must be obtained in non-invasive ways and the biopsies taken from free-ranging animals are a useful tool for toxicological studies. Data on persistent organochlorines (OCs) in sharks and rays are scarce, in manta rays are unknown. Occupying a low trophic level, manta rays could be an early sentinel for the contamination levels in the area. Although many of these persistent organic pollutants are nowadays banned in many countries of the world because of their negative effects on wildlife, they are still found in the environment due to their persistence and slow degradation. Concentrations of OCs such as polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs) and organochlorine pesticides (OCPs) were determined in skin and muscle biopsies of free-ranging oceanic manta rays in Revillagigedo Archipelago and Banderas Bay, where they aggregate in the Mexican Pacific Ocean. Biopsies were taken during scuba and freediving using a pole spear and underwent chemical extraction and subsequent analysis with a gas chromatograph equipped with mass spectrometer (GC-MS) to identify and quantify individual PCB congeners and OCPs. PCBs were detected in biopsies, while no OCPs were detected in any sample. This is the first time that persistent organochlorines are investigated in manta rays and represent a baseline for future studies. OCs can interfere with reproduction in fish and could pose a serious threat to the vulnerable populations of oceanic manta rays around the world.

title: Trace elements concentration in target tissues of a population of lesser spotted dogfish, Scyliorhinus canicula, from Central Mediterranean Sea
abstract_text: Humans, in addition to represent a direct threat to sharks, also indirectly exerts a strong pressure on these animals, due to the continuous release of polluting elements in the water and the atmosphere. Sharks, as predators at the top of marine food chain, act as final receptors for a series of polluting elements that are regularly discharged into the sea. The goal of this research was to delineate and compare trace elements concentration rates in vertebrae, skin and liver of a population of lesser spotted dogfish, Scyliorhinus canicula, from Central Mediterranean. 75 sharks were collected in the Tyrrhenian Sea, 12 miles off of Rocchette Punta Ala. 46 trace elements were analyzed in 75 vertebrae, 12 livers and 12 pieces of skin. Vertebrae were processed with LA-ICPMs, while liver and skin through acid attacks combined with ICPMs. The most abundant and potentially toxic elements were: lead, arsenic, manganese, zinc, nickel, copper, cadmium and iron. Lead, arsenic and manganese showed highest concentrations in the vertebrae, due to the diet of the sharks that is composed of crustaceans, bony fish and shellfish that accumulate many of these elements. Iron and nickel showed highest concentrations in the skin of the samples, due to their presence in the water column, especially along the coast where sharks were collected. At the end, cadmium, zinc and copper showed highest concentrations in the liver, due to their ability to induce trace elements binding metallothionein (MT), which chelates trace metals and reduce the concentration of cadmium.

title: How shiny are shark teeth? Major element quantification in bioapatite
abstract_text: Elasmobranchs are among the most successful vertebrates in the Phanerozoic, with a stratigraphic distribution ranging from the Silurian to Recent times and a global distribution. Like other vertebrates, they share the use of bioapatite in making mineralized tissues. Bioapatite represents a unique archive of physical and chemical environmental information. Indeed, bioapatite lattice can accommodate iso- and hetero-valent substitutions during life or after burial and diagenesis, with a variation of the chemical composition during geological time. Chemical and crystal-chemical data can be achieved by different analytical tools, like laser ablation inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (LA-ICPMS). As LA-ICPMS results are affected by physical-chemical preperties of the sample matrix, an internal standard is usually required to correct and validate the analytical results. Unluckily, an exclusive internal standard is so far missing for bioapatite, strongly affected by isomorphic sobstitutions. A possible solution can be the calibration with external standards which, however, are not so diffused. We propose herein a new method to prepare home-made matrix-matched calibration standards to measure major element concentrations. The method has been tested on living and fossil shark teeth. The final goal is the development of a reliable tool for chemical characterization by LA-ICPMS on small sized samples, avoiding the use of electron microprobe, that is considered a more appropriate technique, but which is more expensive, less diffused and, in any case, once again strictly dependent on the calibrating standards. Our technique can be useful to study teeth of living elasmobranchs in order to find possible chemical and crystal-chemical variation in bioapatite related, for example, to specific habitat, age, gender, etc.

title: Trace elements and isotopes analysis on historical samples of white sharks (Carcharodon carcharias) from central Mediterranean Sea
abstract_text: Both trace elements and isotopes analysis were performed on two samples of vertebrae of White Sharks Carcharodon carcharias from Favignana Island (Sicily, central Mediterranean). For the trace elements analysis, the ICP-MS associated by Laser Ablation allowed us to find 36 trace elements. More samples were taken, on the same vertebrae, along a transect that goes from the most central part of the vertebra to the distal one. Among these 36 trace elements we have been detected high concentrations of Pb, Fe, Zn, Sr, Ba and U. Fluctuations of these elements can be caused by different kind of processes such as variations in temperature, nutrition, uptake of urban pollutants and proximity to industrial areas. The stable isotopes (δ15N and δ13C) analysis has been performed through IRMS (Isotope Ratio Mass Spectrometry) and allowed us to understand the trophic levels of individuals. The two white shark vertebrae showed different isotopic values. The first individual (seven growth layers) presented isotopic ranges from 9.6‰ to 10.8‰ (δ15N) and from -16.5‰ to -13.0‰ (δ13C); this showed a mean ± SD value of 10.3 ± 0.4‰ for δ15N and -14.6 ± 1.3‰ for δ13C. The second individual (five growth layers) presented isotopic ranges from 9.8‰ to 11.1‰ (δ15N) and from -16.9‰ to -15.0‰ (δ13C), displaying a mean ± SD value of 10.8 ± 0.6‰ for δ15N and -15.8 ± 0.8‰ for δ13C. In terms of δ15N values, there were not significant differences (U = 6, p =0.07346) between the two individuals; however, there were significant differences (t = -1.8, p =0.049256) in δ13C values, both at a significance level of 0.05. The absence of differences between the trophic level of the individuals could be related to the trophic level of their preys at the time of age. The differences observed in the case of δ13C are probably correlated to the fact that the first shark was feeding near the coast, while the other feed more offshore.

title: Microbial infection in sharks as a bioindicator for the state of the environment in the eastern Mediterranean Sea
abstract_text: Streptococcus agalactiae (group B streptococcus; GBS) is a zoonotic agent that has a wide range of hosts including both bony and cartilaginous fishes. We describe meningoencephalitis as a result of S. agalactiae (serotype Ia) infection in a female sandbar shark (Carcharhinus plumbeus; Nardo, 1827) that stranded on the eastern Mediterranean coast of Israel in 2018. Based on post-mortem examination, histopathology, and bacterial identification, we conclude that this pathogen was the etiologic agent. C. plumbeus is an endangered (EN) species in the Mediterranean Sea according to the International Union for the Conservation of Nature (IUCN) Red list, with a decreasing number of mature individuals in the population. Information on pathogen prevalence in apex marine predators could inform about potential risks to threatened species and provide indication on the state of the environment in this region. Our findings improve current knowledge about the health status of sharks and warrant further research into the interaction between microbial and high-level organisms in the marine environment.

title: Cartilaginous fish as bioindicator in the Algerian basin
abstract_text: Pollution of marine organisms by heavy metals can occur by direct contamination via the environment or by ingestion of contaminated preys. In order to monitor ecosystems by apprehending their disturbances, it is important to identify bio-indicator species potentially capable of informing about the quality of the environment in which they live. Some sharks and rays as Mustelus sp., Scyliorhinus canicula (Linné, 1758) and Raja sp. may be used as potentially bioindicators. Closely related and part of the same communities, these species occur in the same habitat, each one occupying a distinct ecological niche whose functioning is defined by competition or by prey-predator system. These cartilaginous fish belong to the characteristic community of Diplodus vulgaris (Sparidae). The Thalassa campaign data were used and related to distribution, species diversity and associated fauna. These results are provided by behavioral studies (abundance, spatial distributions, communities), and monitoring of this bony fish, and are also a first step towards the ecosystem approach to fisheries (EAF).

title: Biomagnification of trace elements in the blue shark Prionace glauca in Baja California Sur, Mexico
abstract_text: One of the most abundant and consumed sharks worldwide is the blue shark, Prionace glauca. Due to its high trophic position, it can accumulate large concentrations of potentially toxic elements in its tissues and constitute a risk to human health due to its consumption. As the main route of uptake of trace elements is gastrointestinal, the objective of this study was to determine the biomagnification of mercury (Hg), selenium (Se) and cadmium (Cd) through the main preys of Prionace glauca, on the coast Western Baja California Sur, Mexico. Low average levels of the three trace elements analyzed in the shark muscle tissue were found (Hg = 0.43 ± 0.35 µg g-1 wet weight; Se = 0.53 ± 0.43 µg g-1 dry weight; Cd = 0.24 ± 0.81 µg g-1 wet weight). These values are below the maximum permissible limits so that their meat is suitable for human consumption. Among the female and male individuals no statistically significant differences were found for any of the elements studied. The main prey of the blue shark were the giant squid Dosidicus gigas and the prawn Pleuroncodes planipes, being the latter who provided the greatest contribution of mercury to the blue shark and Dosidicus gigas of selenium. In the case of cadmium, biomagnification did not occur because both preys had higher concentrations of this metal concerning the shark.

title: White blood cells number is correlated to parasitic charge in the small spotted catshark Scyliorhinus canicula
abstract_text: Hematology is now a useful diagnostic tool in human and domestic mammalian medicine and is becoming such also in the clinical evaluation of fish. Most of the current knowledge of fish hematology derives from research carried out on agnate organisms like missine and lampreys, on a few species of elasmobranchs and on some species of teleosts, although standardized hematological methods and reference intervals for elasmobranchs have not yet been established. The goal of this research was to compare the number of white blood cells present in the specimens of a population of lesser spotted dogfish (Scyliorhinus canicula) from central Mediterranean Sea with the parasitic charge. 75 sharks were collected in the Tyrrhenian Sea, 12 miles off of Rocchette Punta Ala, in Tuscany. Helminth communities were analyzed in the stomach, spiral valve, liver, gills, mouth and nostrils of all the sharks collected, while hematological analysis has been performed taking blood samples from venous sinus of the cardiac cavity of 32 sharks. Complete blood analysis has been performed for 10 samples, while for the remaining 22 only the leukocyte count was carried out using the fluorescence flow cytometry method. All the hematological parameters were correlated with each other, but just the correlation between the number of white blood cells and parasitic charge for the 32 sharks considered was extremely significant and inversely proportional, as the parasitized sharks showed fewer white blood cells than the not parasitized ones. The possible explanation of this result can be found in the immunosoppression from accumulation of trace elements (Hg, Pb, Cd, Cu, As, Zn) in the tissues of lesser spotted dogfish, as already demonstrated in some studies carried out on green frogs and bony fish.

title: Vertebrae as novel target for trace elements accumulation in Small-spotted Catshark (Scyliorhinus canicula)
abstract_text: Elasmobranchs are top-predator organisms, essential to maintain trophic web equilibrium in the marine environment. Therefore, fishery and pollutants represent a real threat for these organisms, besides the high lipid content of their diet makes them bioaccumulators organism. Bioaccumulation was previously studied in liver, gills, gut, but little is known about elasmobranch vertebrae. These are an interesting target to study for their structure. Indeed vertebrae are made up of concentric rings, the external are later formed and the inners are the oldest. For this reason, the vertebrae study could allow to evaluate the correlation between pollutants absorption and life traits. Small-Spotted Catshark (Scyliorhinus canicula) was chosen as model because its benthic habits and its ecological importance make it a suitable candidate to study the environmental pollution. Seventy-five specimens were collected in the 'Golfo di Follonica' (Italy). To assess accumulation in vertebrae structure, we analyzed two different parts: the centre and the more external ring. This helped us to denote differences between juvenile and adult stages respectively. Trace element content was assessed through LA-ICP-MS. Results showed a decrease in Pb accumulation during life stages, the same occurred for arsenic and nickel. On the opposite, zinc concentration increases in the external section of vertebra compared to the inner one. This changes could be due to different feeding habits of S. canicula. Indeed, the juveniles feed on small crustaceans and mollusks, organisms known to accumulate arsenic, nickel. On the other hand, adults use to pray fish, with a higher content of Zn. Our data confirm that vertebrae are a reliable marker of pollutant-metals accumulation, and S. canicula is a good candidate for pollution biomonitoring and shark's conservation studies.

title: Shark skin biopsy sampling as a potential non-lethal and less-invasive marine biomonitoring tool
abstract_text: Anthropogenic derived contamination is a daily threat to marine resources. Long-living and slow growing, higher trophic level animals like sharks are usually the most affected. Studies have been made to assess the impacts of contamination on sharks, but they mostly rely on very invasive or even lethal sampling. Non-lethal methods must be developed and optimized, with blood and skin biopsies being already used with some success in large endangered animals like cetaceans. This work aimed to assess the potential of skin biopsies to be used as sole tissues in the assessment of metal contamination and biochemical responses in sharks, using the Atlantic lesser-spotted dogfish (Scyliorhinus canicula) as test species. A total of 74 specimens were captured of the shore of Portugal, aboard a commercial trawling vessel, and sampled for skin and muscle once arrived at the lab (in the same day). A total of 13 metals, along with several energy metabolism and oxidative stress related biochemical responses were measured. Overall, skin tissue tended to harbour greater metallic contamination when compared to muscle. However, positive correlations were found between skin and muscle metal levels, across all tested elements. Biochemical responses, mainly energy metabolism related, also seemed to be similarly influenced by the same metal contaminants in both tissues. All correlations and interactions found in-between metals and biomarkers point to a pattern of similar response both in deeper muscle and skin biopsies. Therefore, this work highlights the potential of skin biopsy to be used as substitute for deeper, more invasive (and lethal) muscle sampling. Studies like this one, encompassing comparisons between sub cellular responses to contamination levels in deeper tissues and skin biopsies, are a crucial and most needed step in validating non-lethal methodologies to be used in future efforts to gather ecotoxicological data and to protect larger endangered shark species.

title: Occurrence of anthropogenic litter in stomach contents of demersal elasmobranchs from the southern Tyrrhenian Sea
abstract_text: To date, available information on marine litter ingestion in Mediterranean elasmobranchs is still very poor, although these species have an important role in the marine trophic web as predators. This study reports the anthropogenic litter ingestion in four elasmobranch species caught by trawlers and longliners in the southern Tyrrhenian Sea: the lesser-spotted dogfish, Scyliorhinus canicula (n= 27; mean total length TL 40.5 ± 6.3 cm), the velvet belly dogfish, Etmopterus spinax (n= 16; mean TL 21.2 ± 7.7 cm), the blackmouth catshark, Galeus melastomus (n= 12; mean TL 20.7 ± 3.0 cm) and the thornback ray Raja clavata (n= 6; mean TL 65.8 ± 2.8 cm). A total of 61 stomach contents were examined by direct visual sorting at a stereo microscope in order to identify the anthropogenic litter. Once isolated, litter particles were counted and categorized by shape, colour and size. Overall, 18 litter particles were identified from the stomach contents of 14 demersal elasmobranchs (23% of total occurrence, O%). In details, litter items were recorded in seven S. canicula (O%= 25.9), four G. melastomus (O%= 33.3), three R. clavata (O%= 50), whereas no litter ingestion was observed in E. spinax. Transparent and white colours resulted the debris with the highest frequency of ingestion (O%= 25). Fragments were the most common litter in stomachs of both S. canicula (O%= 87.5%) and R. clavata (O%= 75), whereas in G. melastomus fragments and filaments occurred with the same frequency (O%= 50). Most litter particles (55.5% of total debris) had a size less than 5 mm. This is the first time that litter ingestion is observed in R. clavata in Mediterranean waters. Some of these species could be considered as indicators for litter ingestion in marine demersal habitats.

title: Morphological and molecular characterization of gastrointestinal parasites in Mustelus mustelus from Adriatic Sea
abstract_text: Increasing interest in the management and conservation of elasmobranchs highlights the importance of acquiring further knowledge of their biology and ecology; in this respect, important information can be derived from the analysis of their parasite fauna. Parasitological investigations focused on elasmobranchs from Mediterranean Sea are scarce; the compilation of accurate and updated checklists is further complicated by the occurrence of old records of infection and the doubtful identity of the shark host. A healthy specimen of Common Smoothhound, Mustelus mustelus, (total length: 66 cm) fished as bycatch in northern Adriatic Sea was subjected to a complete parasitological examination. Collected parasites were processed for morphological and morphometric analyses aimed at identifying them to the species level. Parasite identity was confirmed through amplification and sequencing of 28S rDNA. Nematodes belonging to the species Acanthocheilus rotundatus (15 specimens) were recovered from the stomach and the proximal intestine, while cestodes belonging to the species Calliobothrium verticillatum (5 specimens) were collected from the spiral valve. Calliobothrium spp. are known to parasitize different species of Mustelus around the world's oceans. Particularly, C. verticillatum has been reported in M. mustelus from Northeastern Atlantic and only one report dating back to the 50s on this parasite in M. mustelus from Mediterranean Sea exists. Our results would therefore confirm the occurrence of this host-parasite association in Mediterranean waters. Acanthocheilus rotundatus has been described infecting M. mustelus from Adriatic Sea based on morphological evidence; our work provides the first sequence data of A. rotundatus from Mediterranean Sea, since only sequences of specimens collected in extra-Mediterranean areas were available so far. Updated knowledge on the parasite fauna of M. mustelus from Adriatic Sea would contribute to elucidate aspects of the ecology, biology and health status of elasmobranchs from Mediterranean Sea, providing useful information for their proper management and conservation.

title: Forty-five years of shark conservation: from "Jaws" to 2019
abstract_text: Jaws, the novel, was published in 1974 and the film released in 1975. Forty-five years ago, about 800 species of sharks, rays and chimaeras were known to science and the global human population was around 4 billion. Today, about 1,250 chondrichthyan fishes have been described and the human population is roughly 7.5 billion. This presentation reviews the history of shark conservation and management since the 1970s and current challenges faced as the year 2020 approaches.

title: Use of genomics for applied elasmobranch conservation
abstract_text: The advent of Next Generation Sequencing (NGS) technologies has seen a transition from conservation genetics to genomics (from gene to genome scales), which is informing our understanding of species and improving conservation outcomes based on these insights. This technology has provided access to thousands of genome-wide markers, collectively capable of providing reliable inferences about demographic patterns and enabling detection of local adaptation. Examples of applied genomics in elasmobranch conservation and forensics at different levels, from species to individuals are becoming more common as we develop genomic resources for non-model species. For species identification, when diagnostic external morphological characters are lacking, or when identifications rely on body parts, the use of non-expensive techniques such as mtDNA sequencing is often used. However, when dealing with closely related, recently diverged species, as is the case of the Galapagos (Carcharhinus galapagensis) and dusky (C. obscurus) sharks, the combination of mtDNA and genome-wide diagnostic markers is required to distinguish the species. This also allows other biologically relevant patterns of genetic variation to be explored, such as those that arise due to hybridization. A first population connectivity assessment of C. galapagensis in the Eastern Tropical Pacific resulted in the development of 1,873 high-resolution SNP markers. A selected subset of SNPs was further used to successfully assess hybridisation patterns between this, and C. obscurus. Future steps include the use of such markers as forensic tools to develop a cost-effective PCR-based essay to rapidly distinguish the two species from carcases or body parts. Likewise, the development of worldwide genomic resources capable of detecting population structure at large as well as fine geographic scales is crucial at the population level to identify particular signatures of selection and local adaptation that can lead to provenience-detecting markers. Finally, at the individual level the inference of the sex-determination systems in new species is leading the way towards the identification of sex-linked markers that can aid sex identification from fin or tissue samples. Current efforts using in silico and PCR validations are showing that SNP markers can be effective at assigning the correct sex in at least twelve of the sixteen species tested. Applying fundamental knowledge towards the development of molecular traceability tools is the logical and much needed step towards shark conservation.

title: A world platform to support data collection on endangered shark species in the Mediterranean Sea
abstract_text: In the Mediterranean Sea, sharks are currently one of the less frequently observed groups of animals. Scientific surveys do not provide enough observation effort to collect relevant data on the presence and distribution of the species, and fisheries data have been historically scattered and rarely adequate in terms of taxonomic resolution. Following the IUCN regional assessment 57% of the species are listed as endangered and 25 % as still data deficient. New monitoring strategies need to take place in the area to improve data collection, and new technologies can create a link between people and scientists. Data management is crucial in these cases. Here we present sharkPulse, a collaborative international project aiming to involve divers, fishermen, surfers, beachgoers and other ocean users in sharing image-based sightings of sharks. To facilitate users participation the sharkPulse team has developed a web platform (http:\\sharkpulse.org) and a mobile application (IOS and Android). All the data collected are available and shared online with summary tables and distribution maps. To break linguistic barriers and boost participation, the project has created national focal points in several parts of the world (Italy, UK, New Zealand, South Africa, Greece). From 2016, the Italian national focal point has focused his activity on the Mediterranean Sea, collecting more than 900 photographic records of 35 shark species. Here we present a first exploration of these data and highlight some emerging patterns: i) possible identification of strongholds for rare and endangered species; ii) seasonal shifts in pelagic shark distributions; and iii) presence of newborns and immature specimens for broad-ranging species such as the shortfin mako (Isurus oxyrinchus) for which these sightings are more frequent (75% of the records) than adults. Integrated collection and analysis of these data can improve scientific understanding of sharks in the Mediterranean Sea, fill the data gap that has historically characterized the basin on these species, and stimulate conservation and recovery actions.

title: Shark and Ray Forensics, a conservation tool for the Western Indian Ocean region
abstract_text: Worldwide, ocean and coastal threat is driven by the rapid expansion of fisheries and global trade markets, whereby overfishing activities and habitat degradation have severely altered elasmobranch populations. The western Indian Ocean is an important conservation area for sharks and rays as this region is a global hotspot for biodiversity and for threatened species. The harvesting of elasmobranchs in this region is amongst others driven by the international shark meat and shark fin trade. In this study, we assessed marine forensics as a tool for complementing traditional identification methods – through the development of a mini-barcoding assay as well as High Resolution Melt (HRM) analysis, relevant to elasmobranch species occurring in the western Indian Ocean region. This involved the testing and optimisation of the standard barcoding region of the cytochrome oxidase c subunit 1 (COI), using traditional barcoding primers as well as two sets of nested PCR primers in a multiplex assay. Preliminary results (only a 22% species identification success rate) indicated the limitations of using only the traditional COI primers and warrented the inclusion of additional gene regions for species identification of future shark forensic cases. In this study, a mini-barcoding multiplex assay comprising three primer sets were optimised and applied to a wide range of shark forensic case studies, involving confiscated shark fins possibly for illegal trade. Furthermore, a HRM approach was validated based on six southern African houndshark species and further optimised for additional commercially exploited species such as hammerhead S. lewini and S. zygaena, copper C. brachyurus, dusky C. obscurus, bull C. leucas, blacktip C. limbatus and blue shark P. glauca. Ultimately, these approaches can be combined to develop a relatively fast and cost-effective identification protocol that can be applied to identify most, if not all, elasmobranch species involved in trade regionally.

title: Reducing bycatch and mortality in the Med: the project proposal eLIFE (elasmobranch low impact fishing experience)
abstract_text: Over-exploitation and fishery by-catch leads to an increasing decline of elasmobranchs worlwide; with unpredictable consequences for the health and structure of the ecosystems. According to IUCN, the Mediterranean Sea is amongst the three top regions where the biodiversity of sharks and rays is seriously threatened. Considering the European waters, the IUCN reveals that half of the assessed elasmobranch species, 39 out of 73, are threatened at Mediterranean level. Despite some recent efforts in EU to reduce shark by-catch and mortality (i.e., adoption of the European Commission's Action plan for the Conservation and Management of Sharks, and adoption of the Council Regulation (EU) 2017/127), the EC goals are far from being achieved, and conservation actions need to be set up. Current legislation only prevents retention and trade, but not the actual capture or the mortality that may occur as a result. The factors that contribute to the by-catch and the mortality of elasmobranch during fisheries capture are - in fact - many, but the major is the fishers' attitude. The consciuous and responsible behavior of the employees in commercial fishing activities is fundamental to mitigate the impact of their actions on the marine biodiversity, cartilaginous fishes included. The project eLIFE (elasmobranch low impact fishing experience), has been recently funded by the EU's LIFE programme for the protection of the enviornment. It aims to reduce the elasmobranch by-catch and mortality by promoting best conservation practices in the context of the EU commercial fishing activities in the Mediterranean Sea. It targets several sharks listed as endengered or critically endengered in the Red List of the European marine fishes of the IUCN and it includes the partecipation of 3 EU countries (Italy, Cyprus and Greece). eLIFE is based on the direct involvement of the professional fishers, and will test the efficiency of using low impact fishing gears and correct methods of manipulation for the elasmobranch incidental caught, as well as the use of digital technology, like satellite tags and a smartphone application to monitor the efficency of the conservation actions and to obtain new spatial information.

title: How key stakeholders can help secure the future of the Critically Endangered Angelshark
abstract_text: The Angelshark (Squatina squatina) was once widespread throughout the Eastern Atlantic and Mediterranean Sea, but now is one of the most threatened fish in European waters. Indeed, the angel shark family is identified as the second most threatened elasmobranch taxon after a global review of extinction risk by the IUCN. A unique stronghold remains for the Angelshark in the Canary Islands, but even here the species is under threat. Given the importance of forging bonds with key stakeholders to secure the future of this species, Angel Shark Project: Canary Islands (ASP:CI), a collaboration between Universidad de Las Palmas de Gran Canaria, Zoological Society of London and Zoologisches Forschungsmuseum Alexander Koenig, has developed a number of tools to engage interested parties and encourage them to provide information to aid scientific research. Our focus is on the recreational sector, specifically divers and fishers. This year, ASP:CI has re-launched best practice guidelines in collaboration with the recreational fishing sector to a) encourage fishers to safely release any accidentally caught Angelsharks, b) report these encounters and c) gain the trust of the fishing community and raise the awareness on the species. In addition, we completed the first Count the Angels event in Fuerteventura, which brings together dive centres to complete a census of Angelsharks across the island via coordinated diving. A total of 7 dive centres participated, 24 Angelsharks sighted and over 882 diving hours were completed during this event. This not only reinforces the bond with the diving community, but enables greater coverage across large stretches of coastline to better understand Angelshark presence, and in the future, calculate abundance metrics. These tools will ensure and reinforce the bond between scientists and the recreational community, a key task when working with a Critically Endangered species.

title: Longline fishery in a marine reserve – catching protected megafauna in the Galapagos Islands
abstract_text: Marine megafauna (elasmobranchs, mammals, turtles, birds) is important from an ecological point of view because it occupies upper trophic levels and is also often essential for marine tourism. Species belonging to this group are often heavily impacted by fishing due to their longevity, late sexual maturity and low reproductive output, which affect the capability to recover from depletion. In the Galapagos, marine megafauna is protected throughout the marine reserve and is the main attraction for marine tourism, generating millions of dollars in revenue annually. Multiple artisanal longlining projects were carried out since the 1990s with the aim of redirecting fishing effort from the depleted coastal-demersal species to pelagic fish, such as yellowfin tuna, Thunnus albacares and swordfish, Xiphias gladius. All these projects have resulted in high bycatch of megafauna. Despite its importance in the archipelago, megafauna is still being caught as bycatch in the longline fishery, without independent scientific studies to evaluate its impact, largely due to poor objective definition, data collection, and enforcement. To fill in this knowledge gap, we analyzed data of the fifth longline fishing project (2012-2013) to describe the fishery, identify variables affecting bycatch, and suggest mitigation strategies. This experimental project involved twelve fishing vessels, which deployed 42,007 hooks catching 4,893 individuals belonging to 33 species, mostly yellowfin tuna. Of those, 16 species were protected megafauna, particularly blacktip sharks, Carcharhinus limbatus and oceanic manta, Manta birostris. These species were regularly captured during the two fishing seasons and in all the four bioregions that occur in the archipelago, suggesting little potential to mitigate their catch. As an alternative, we identified 14 hotspots where yellowfin tuna and swordfish could be harvested through more selective fishing techniques. In an archipelago where the main economic activity is marine wildlife tourism, the implementation of an extractive and unselective activity such as pelagic longline fishing should be avoided to ensure the preservation of the Galapagos marine ecosystem and its booming tourism industry.

title: Using local ecological knowledge to reconstruct trends in elasmobranch populations in the Strait of Sicily
abstract_text: Fishers have a rich knowledge of the resources and the environment in which they work, that is rarely utilised to provide advice on the status of exploited populations. Fishers "local ecological knowledge" (LEK) can be used to reconstruct species trends, like sharks, that currently are at very low biomass due to overfishing. In this study we used the historical memories of Sicilian fishers to gather data on change in fishing practices and capture of cartilaginous species in the Strait of Sicily over the last decades. We conducted interviews with 27 retired trawl fishers from Mazara del Vallo harbour (SW Sicily) using a pre-defined questionnaire with a series of open and fixed questions and comparing to the present abundance. The questionnaire included specific questions about the trends they perceived in cartilaginous fish occurence abundance between 1940s and 2000s (according to three main time periods 1940-1960, 1961-1980 and 1981-2010), in order to facilitate the estimation of eventual changes over time. A total of 29 species were mentioned by fishermen during interviews, including large pelagic sharks (Carcharhinidae, Sphyrnidae and Lamnidae), mesopredatory demersal sharks (Squalidae, Hexanchidae, Centrophoridae, Oxynotidae, Triakidae, Scyliorhinidae and Squatinidae) and batoids. Overall shark catches were perceived to have diminished since the early 1940s: about 95% of fishers reported the decline of commercially important species (e.g. Mustelus spp.) and indicated species that could have been depleted (e.g. Squatina spp., Sphyrna spp.). Our study shows that LEK of fishers can be beneficial for reconstructing long-term population trends of exploited species when traditional standard data on fisheries catch or species relative abundance from surveys is limited or only available for recent periods. The results obtained cleary indicate the rapid and alarming decline of elasmobranchs in the Strait of Sicily highlighting the need for urgent conservation measures to be adopted.

title: Molecular identification of endangered marine predators by barcoding ancient museum rostra of Mediterranean sawfish populations
abstract_text: A growing concern in conserving threatened animals affected by human impact has been significant worldwide. Among marine animals, sawfishes (Chondrichthyes, Pristidae) are considered one of the most endangered families among elasmobranchs, resulting in extinction in many coastal areas around the world, including the Mediterranean Sea. Here, sawfish occurred with two species, Pristis pristis and P. pectinata, until the second half of the last century and are now considered Critically Endangered/Possibly Extinct. The historical occurrence of sawfish in the area is documented by bibliographic/ archival records and numerous preserved historical rostra available in museum collections. In this study we attempted to genetically characterize the historical remains of sawfish from several European museums and to enable, in the future, the preliminary investigation of their evolutionary and ecological relationships with global samples. A total of 80 rostra specimens, dated from 1813 to 1959 and catalogued as unknown origin or Mediterranean (11), were collected from 11 European museums and were properly prepared for ancient DNA genetic analysis. Taxonomic identification at the species level was obtained through PCR amplification of small fragments (150 bp) of two mitochondrial markers commonly used for species identification (i.e., the mitochondrial COI and the NADH2). Sequence comparison with currently available ones from public repositories and phylogenetic tree analyses indicated that the historical specimens belonged to four species, P. pristis, P. zijsron, P. pectinata, and Anoxypristis cuspidata, with a high frequency of mismatches (69%) between molecular identification and species museum cataloguing, when present. These preliminary data also showed the presence of two sequence sub-clusters in the poorly barcoded species P. zijsron. With the expansion of this initial analysis, we will contribute to increase the limited molecular data of these critically endangered large predators and to exploit historical genetic data for reconstructing phylogenetic/phylogeographic extent of the possibly extinct population of Mediterranean sawfish.

title: Involving stakeholders in the evaluation of Atlantic shark fisheries management strategies and why they matter to sharks
abstract_text: Shortfin-mako (Isurus oxyrinchus) and blue shark (Prionace glauca) are the two most captured pelagic shark species in the Atlantic Ocean. Since 1990 Spanish longline fleet has been registered for the highest by-cacth of both species in the Atlantic Ocean. About shortfin-mako, concern has been raised after the last evaluation for the northern Atlantic in 2017 made by ICCAT and the stock assessment update meeting held in 2019. It stated the population being overfished and suffering from overfishing. About blue shark, although capture levels appear to be within sustainable fishing limits, it is subject to high exploitation rates in the Atlantic. Uncertainties in assessment results suggest that additional management actions could be considered for both species. In this study different fisheries management strategies were evaluated for shortfin-mako and blue shark in the Atlantic from the stakeholder’s perspective. Local Ecological Knowledge (LEK) was considered to be useful as fishermen possess a unique knowledge based on their continued interaction with the species and the environment. Information was collected through personal interviews with fishermen from the Spanish longline fleet and surveys sent out to scientists and NGOs. Interviews allowed to collect fishermen’s observations on variations of abundance, distribution patterns, size of capture and seasonal fluctuations for both species. SWOT-analysis was used to study the different factors to be taken into account for various management measures. Main management strategies proposed by stakeholders were time-area closure, especially for blue shark juveniles during the summer months in the Sole Bank, minimum capture size and a quota system. This study suggests that management could be supported by involving stakeholders due to their knowledge about the species and environment. Lastly, observations of fishermen about ecological features of both species could be used as a valid aid for future scientific studies.

title: SharkPulse: taking the pulse of global shark populations
abstract_text: Many species of sharks and their relatives are declining worldwide at a rapid rate because of their vulnerable life histories exposed to impacts of fishing and habitat modification. For this reason, they are among the most endangered animals in the ocean. Meanwhile, they are also the most poorly quantified groups of animals in the ocean as basic information on abundance and distribution is lacking for about half of their species. Lack of data is hampering conservation assessment and policy actions and has thus become one of the biggest issues for shark conservation. Available solutions for developing effective conservation actions and reverse loss include exploring alternative sources of information and unconventional methods to collect and analyze abundance and distribution data. Here we show how to transition from data deficient to big data for many shark species. By taking advance of the surge of information on human ocean use and communication, we show how crowdsourcing, web data-mining and machine learning can fill this critical information gap. We integrated these approaches in a modular crowd-sourcing platform that combines social network and web site crawling, web applications, smartphone technology, and image analysis to build the largest database of shark sighting available today. We will show how these data can be used to produce species distribution and models to inform conservation assessments and promote protection and recovery plans.

title: Spatial variability of Chondrichthyes in the North Mediterranean
abstract_text: Thanks to the availability of the MEDITS survey data, a picture of the occurrence, abundance and distribution of Chondrichthyes in the Mediterranean basin was done. During the spring-summer MEDITS period (2012-2015), 41 Chondrichthyes, including 18 sharks (5 Orders and 10 Families), 22 batoids (3 Orders and 4 Families) and 1 chimaera, were detected from several Geographical Subareas (GSAs). In general, it is possible to observe that batoid species had a preferential distribution in the shelf (10-200 m) while “shark” species were more frequent in the slope (200-800 m). Only three species, the Carcharhiniformes Galeus melastomus, Scyliorhinus canicula and the Torpediniformes Torpedo marmorata were caught in all several GSAs studied. On the shelf, the Rajidae family was represented in primis by Raja clavata and then by R. miraletus, R. polystigma and R. asterias. The slope was characterized by the prevalence of the blackmouth catshark G. melastomus in all GSAs followed by S. canicula, E. spinax and Squalus blainville. Throughout a comparison between the maps of trawling fishing pressure in Mediterranean (Sbrana et al., 2013) and our maps of abundance’s species it is clear that the most affected areas, as Adriatic sea and Spanish areas (with the exception of the Baleares islands) registered low abundance of Elasmobranchs but other areas with high level of pressure, as the South western of Sicily, presented high level of abundance, showing that, in this case, other environmental drivers work together with the fishing pressure to define the levels of biomass and density. Results of Generalized Additive Models (GAM) highlighted the depth range (followed by the temperature) as one of the most important drivers influencing the distribution of both batoid and shark species.

title: “Winners & Losers”, a vulnerability analysis of sharks, rays and chimaeras in the Gulf of California (GoC), Mexico
abstract_text: Fisheries contribute to food security and poverty alleviation, particularly in developing countries such as Mexico. Therefore, it is important to assess the risks to fisheries resources in a comprehensive way. The vulnerability analysis of 106 species of pelagic, coastal and demersal chondrichthyans in the Gulf of California area performed in this study involves two regions (the southern and entrance), two timescales (2050 and 2099), four types of fishing and eight climate change stressors. The risk from fishing stressors is related to exposure to the demersal prawn fishery, the artisanal fishery, the industrial shark fishery, and the sardine fishery from 2006 to 2017, also depending on the species’ productivity and susceptibility. The risk from climate change stressors was assessed by how species are likely to be affected by eight climate change stressors (rising water temperature, increasing storm frequency and intensity, changing currents and upwelling, increasing salinity, decreasing DO and chlorophyll-a and increasing ocean acidity). The assessment was based on the species’ sensitivity and adaptability to changing habitats and on indicators of what may happen based on IPCC emissions scenarios for the area by 2100. We have assessed which species of chondrichthyans are likely to be highly affected (“Losers”) and those considered “Winners” by assigning each species to six ecological groups (EGs) (a novel and flexible way to allocate a great number of species) based on species’ lifestyle and habitat. The EGs of shelf-inshore, shelf-reef and shelf-sand (≤75 m) are likely to have high exposure risk to the climate change stressors under medium and high emission scenarios, whereas exposure risk from fishing stressors was high for the EGs of shelf-inshore and shelf-sand (≤75 m) in both regions.

title: Toxic soup: Fins from top traded shark species in Hong Kong and China found not recommended for human consumption
abstract_text: The trade of shark-derived products is a primary driver of the decline in shark populations globally. Shark fin is one of China’s top dried seafood products and, with over 80 shark species currently present in the Hong Kong (HK) trade, shark fin soup is an asian delicacy on high demand. The high position of sharks in marine food webs and their relatively long life spans mean that they can often have high concentrations of heavy metals in their tissues. Heavy metals including mercury (Hg), Methylmercury (MeHg), lead (Pb), arsenic (As), cadmium (Cd) and selenium (Se) all have adverse health effects on humans, especially in pregnant women and children. Shark meat contains high values of Hg, often surpassing the recommended human consumption advisory limits. To date, little is known about the risks of consuming shark fin products on a regular basis, and virtually no studies have addressed this issue. Here, we analyze processed shark fins from the China and HK markets (n=267) for Hg, MeHg, Pb, As, Cd and Se to obtain novel information on their heavy metal concentrations and to inform consumers of the risks of ingesting fins from a suite of species (n=9) currently heavily traded. Results indicate all shark species in the study are above maximum consumption Hg limits established by HK and US EPA. A complex of Blacktip species, Carcharhinus longimanus, Prionace glauca, Sphyrna lewini and Sphyrna Zygaena all surpass the European comission’s Hg limits (1ppm) and WHO/JECFA’s MeHg potential tolerable weekly intake (1.6 𝜇gMeHg/kg bw). P. glauca samples were found to surpass inorganic As maximum levels established by WHO/JECFA (70.59% samples > 3 𝜇giAs/kg bw ). Results show high inter and intra-specific variation in Hg, As and MeHg concentrations, as well as low Cd, Se and Pb concentrations for the majority of individuals.

title: Baselines for butterfly babies: towards a mediteranean study model
abstract_text: The spiny butterfly ray, Gymnura altavela, is a benthic batoid found on soft bottoms in shallow coastal waters in the Atlantic Ocean and the Mediterranean Sea, where it is considered a Critically Endangered species on certain areas of its distribution. As G. altavela is a species with a patchy and discontinuous distribution, the identification, characterization and protection of its congregation areas may be the key issue for the future of the species. Its big size, calmed behaviour and presence in beaches with a high tourist activity make this species an emblematic animal for conservation plans. To evaluate this purpose, a series of monthly surveys were conducted during a year in areas located in Alicante (South-Eastern Spain) with different level of tourism. In each survey, the number of spiny butterfly ray marks found in the sediment with its length, width and location depth were recorded. Live animals found were also measured in length and width, and pictures of the pectoral fins and tail were taken for photoidentification. A total of 26 different alive animals were found during the daily surveys, showing a disc width range of 77-112 cm for males and 53-157 cm for females. The alive specimens found were resting on the bottom covered by sediment beside seagrass meadows of Posidonia oceanica or Cymodocea nodosa. Only juvenile specimens (<64 cm width) were found resting in sand patches within C. nodosa meadows. The occurrence of females was constant throughout the year, while male occurrence was higher in spring. During the period October-June, coinciding with the months of less tourism, spiny butterfly ray specimens and its marks were observed in all the surveyed areas, whereas during June-September period, coinciding with the tourism season, no animals or its marks could be observed in the areas with high level of tourism activities.
